title: Boyhood friends, Willie Foster, Oklahoma musicians and Chinatown
summary: One long reminiscence: growing up with the Humphreys, Foster leaving, Joe Oliver's call, Oklahoma players, and working at Chinatown and the 1937 contest.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: the name? Where he's from? Oh well, my mother was born and growing up with Virginia. You understand? They came here from Virginia. She was a, what you call a practical nurse and they come down here. Well, it was a lady who used to live on 2nd Street, or Phillips City Street, I believe it was, Miss Cecilia Logan. She used to be the head training nurse at Hotel Duke. Well, she got my mother's job nursing, Chief O'Connor. Chief O'Connor was the chief of police at that time, you understand? And got her nursing around there like that. So, uh, uh, Mr. Eliza Green used to live on, the house was still running on, on Robinson between gender and kids, who used to keep Poissy Humphrey in Iowa while my mother worked and went to school. His aunt, Poissy's aunt. You see, after Poissy's mother died, well, he died when he was small with Poissy and I were practically read up together. He's about your age? Yeah, Poissy should be. Might be older than me. A lot of them fellas don't tell the age. I didn't have mine correct, but I mean I got it straightened out, you know, what I meant to say, Poissy and Willie and Oil, we all came up together. I see. You see, but they were older than I was, but you see, and I went to his granddaddy to take some lessons, but he was more acquainted with the violin. And I always had ideas thirty years ahead. That's what everybody say. Always had modern ideas. So I got with Willie Foster. You see, Willie Foster's pop Foster's brother. You understand? Oh yeah. The bass player. You know, he was out there in California. And, well, I got with Willie died. He died in Baton Rouge, about a year or so ago. And he left here. He lived in 8510 Corn Street. Well he had trouble with his wife, you know, like men do. You have trouble with some things like that. And he put me in an awkward position, because just at the time I thought I was getting good, you know, I was required to have a teacher to lead me on. He had to move on. Well I got Mr. Boyto, his ideas were different, but music is music. You understand? And he learned from me. Well you know, and then I started going up and down the road, playing music with different bands. So therefore it caused me to go. I was supposed to play with Joe Oliver. They had sent for me. Myrick Kennedy was working with him then. And they had sent for me. I got to play Oklahoma and I got to meet the great Charlie Christie. Well that's a town similar to New Orleans, you know, and I met Bell and a lot of fellas, we used to jam at our off time. Well I was, he met who? Bell. Bell, he plays bass with Duke now. They were down there. Aaron Bell. Bell, he was a sister, he used to play trumpet but he's on bass now. And he had a sister who played piano. And we, they were living down here. We were you know, at Willie Humphrey's aunt's house. Emory, big Emory. Emory's house. Yeah. Emory's house. Compton. Compton. Yeah, out there on Liberty Street. Well, we used to get together and Wes and Bostick, they came down there. Well, Bostick wound up living with Joe Rovershue down on Magnolia and there on Louie's Avenue. And when they was back at the Rhythm Club. When they was at the Rhythm Club, I was at Chinatown. And then Handy and Son Johnson and all that, and Smiley and Joe, well he wasn't, he was mostly an entertainer, singing. But I was at Chinatown and Miss Isabel Osborne was the lead proprietor of Chinatown. Well, I was working there. Well, I was working there. But before I come there, I was working down at the Roseland, those Delphys down on Caryope and, and, and, um, Lowell they called it, Franklin at that time, but they called it Lowell. And I worked in that club and then I come, come up to Chinatown. And then I went back to the entertainers, and after the entertainers went up, out of business. down there and I come back to Chinatown and I've been playing fraternity houses all up down Broadway, all in different places. And Dalton Richards, a while he had a little combo, I was in and out with him. And then 1937 they had all the bands in the city, Joe Robichaud, Professor Victor, and Sidney Desvignes, Salestand, and all the bands in the city. 1937, I won the swing contest out the city, back on, at St. Monica's, back on Poison, Galveston.
